title: Calisthenics
wiki_lead:
Calisthenics (American English) or callisthenics (British English) (, also known as bodyweight exercises) is a form of strength training that utilizes an individual's body weight as resistance to perform multi-joint, compound movements with little or no equipment. Calisthenics are popular for their convenience, as they require little to no equipment and can be performed anywhere.
Calisthenics can enhance a range of biomotor abilities including strength, power, endurance, speed, flexibility, coordination and balance. Such strength training has become more popular among recreational and professional athletes. Calisthenics use simple abilities like pushing, pulling, squatting, bending, twisting and balancing. Movements such as the push-up, the pull-up, and the sit-up are among the most common calisthenic exercises.

Such strength training has become more popular among recreational and professional athletes. Calisthenics use simple abilities like pushing, pulling, squatting, bending, twisting and balancing. Movements such as the push-up, the pull-up, and the sit-up are among the most common calisthenic exercises.


Origin and etymology
The Oxford English Dictionary describes calisthenics as "gymnastic exercises to achieve fitness and grace of movement". The word calisthenics comes from the ancient Greek words κάλος (kállos), which means "beauty", and σθένος (sthenos), meaning "strength".
The practice was recorded as being used in ancient Greece, including by the armies of Alexander the Great and the Spartans at the Battle of Thermopylae.
Calisthenics was also recorded to have been used in ancient China. Along with dietary practices, Han dynasty physicians prescribed calisthenics as one of the methods for maintaining one's health.


Common exercises
The more commonly performed calisthenic exercises include:
Push-ups
Performed face down on the floor, palms against the floor under the shoulders, toes curled upwards against the floor. The arms are used to lift the body while maintaining a straight line from head to heel. The arms go from fully extended in the high position to nearly fully flexed in the low position while avoiding resting on the floor. This exercise trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps. An easier version of this exercise consists of placing the hands on a wall and then bending and straightening the arms.
Sit-ups
A person lies on their back with their legs bent. They bend at the waist and move their head and torso towards their legs. They then lower themselves back down to the start position. For people who find it difficult to get down onto the ground, a similar range of motion can be achieved by standing with the legs slightly bent, and then bowing slightly and straightening up again.
Curl-ups
The curl-up or crunch is an abdominal exercise that works the rectus abdominis muscle.

Squats
Standing with the feet a shoulder-width apart, the subject squats down until their thighs are parallel with the floor; during this action, they move their arms forwards in front of them. They then return to a standing position whilst moving their arms back to their sides. Squats train the quadriceps, hamstrings, calves, gluteal muscles, and core. It was coined in the early 19th century, first attested in 1842, initially referring to light gymnastic exercises aimed at women to promote graceful movement, figure development, and fitness. The practice itself has ancient roots in ancient Greece (used by Spartans and Alexander the Great's armies), China, and India for building strength and health. In ancient Greek culture, these exercises were integral to Olympic training, military preparation, and daily life to promote self-empowerment and overall wellness. The modern revival began in the late 18th century with Pehr Henrik Ling, who developed Swedish Gymnastics incorporating calisthenic principles for health prevention and rehabilitation, influencing the Physical Culture movement from 1890 to 1925. By the early 20th century, calisthenics had gained widespread popularity in educational and fitness programs before being partially overshadowed by weight-based bodybuilding. Common calisthenic exercises include push-ups, pull-ups, squats, planks, jumping jacks, and lunges, which target multiple muscle groups simultaneously and can be adapted for various fitness levels. These exercises often have descriptive names that directly describe the physical action, body position, or movement performed, making them easy to understand, teach, and communicate universally without relying on equipment, inventors, or abstract terms. These movements enhance muscular strength, cardiovascular fitness, balance, and flexibility. Calisthenics supports fat loss and weight management through elevated calorie expenditure from dynamic, compound movements and by promoting muscle development, which increases resting metabolic rate. Beginners can build significant muscle mass in 3-4 months through consistent calisthenics training, progressive overload (e.g., advancing to harder variations, increasing repetitions, or training close to failure), and adequate nutrition, with hypertrophy comparable to traditional weight training in some cases, particularly for beginners and certain muscle groups such as the upper body and lower body in sedentary individuals. Studies have shown comparable increases in muscle thickness and strength from progressive bodyweight training to weighted training over short periods. However, neither calisthenics nor weight training enables spot reduction of fat in specific areas such as the abdomen; effective fat loss requires an overall caloric deficit, primarily achieved through diet. Calisthenics is highly accessible for beginners, including those over 40 and those with higher body fat, as it requires no equipment and can be performed anywhere. It is suitable and effective for beginners over 40, focusing on proper form, modifications (e.g., knee push-ups, assisted pull-ups), and gradual progressions to build strength safely while protecting joints. It is advisable to consult a doctor before beginning, especially with prior injuries or medical conditions. While weight training may provide advantages in progressive overload for advanced muscle building, specific muscle isolation, and preservation during caloric deficits, calisthenics is highly effective for beginners and home-based training; combining both modalities is often ideal for optimizing strength, muscle mass, and long-term fat reduction. These benefits make calisthenics suitable for home or outdoor settings, including small spaces, without specialized gear. Research indicates that regular calisthenic training can improve muscle force steadiness, dynamic balance, and overall physical function, particularly when integrated into routines to break up sedentary time. In contemporary contexts, calisthenics has evolved into competitive street workout sports, emphasizing skill-based progressions like muscle-ups and human flags, while remaining a foundational element of general fitness programs.
